content:
We need to propose a retrosynthesis route with 1 reaction (i.e., one step) to synthesize target molecule. The target SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

Simplify: It's an alkene attached to phenyl and a cyclopentanol with CF3 group? Actually C15 with three Fs is CF3 attached to carbon 15 which is part of the cyclopentane? The structure: a cyclopentane (C9-10-11-12-13) with OH on C13 and CF3 on C15? Wait C15 is attached to C13? The SMILES: ...[C@@H]1[CH2][CH2][CH2][C@@]1([OH])[C]([F])([F])[F]. So a cyclopentane where one carbon (C13) is attached to OH and also attached to CF3 group (C15). So it's a tertiary alcohol? Actually C13 is attached to OH and to CF3 carbon (C15) which is CF3. So it's a tertiary alcohol with CF3 substituent.

The retrosynthetic step likely is a carbonyl-ene reaction: forward reaction is carbonyl-ene forming the product (our target). So retrosynthesis: break the C-O bond to give a ketone and an alkene? The carbonyl-ene reaction: starting from a ketone and an alkene (with allylic hydrogen) to give an allylic alcohol (product). So reverse: our target (allylic alcohol) can be derived from a ketone precursor (same skeleton but carbonyl instead of OH) and an alkene (maybe same as internal). The carbonyl-ene reaction forms a new C-C bond between the carbonyl carbon and the alkene's terminal carbon, and moves the double bond.

Thus the retrosynthetic disconnection: break the C-O bond to give a ketone (maybe a cyclopentanone with CF3) and an alkene (maybe the same phenyl-substituted alkene). Actually the product has an alkene attached to phenyl and to the carbon bearing the cyclopentane. In carbonyl-ene, the alkene is external, reacting with carbonyl to give allylic alcohol. So the precursor could be a ketone where the carbonyl carbon is attached to the cyclopentane (C13) and the alkene is separate (maybe a phenyl-substituted alkene). The product's double bond is between C1 and C2 (CH2= C attached to phenyl and to C9). In product, C2 is attached to phenyl and to C9 (the cyclopentane). In carbonyl-ene, the double bond moves to the carbonyl carbon? Let's think: carbonyl-ene: R-CH=CH2 + R'C=O -> R-CH-CH2-CH(OH)-R' (allylic alcohol). The new C-C bond formed between the alkene's terminal carbon (CH2) and the carbonyl carbon. The double bond shifts to internal position between the other alkene carbon and the allylic carbon. So in product, the double bond is between the internal alkene carbon and the allylic carbon (which becomes attached to OH). In our product, the double bond is between CH2 (C1) and C2 which is attached to phenyl and to C9 (the cyclopentane). The OH is on C13 (on cyclopentane). Wait the OH is not on the double bond carbon; it's on the cyclopentane carbon (C13). So maybe the carbonyl-ene formed a bond between the carbonyl carbon (C13) and the terminal carbon of the alkene (C1). The OH ends up on C13 (the carbonyl carbon becomes alcohol). The double bond shifts to between C2 and C9? Actually product double bond is between C1 and C2, not between C2 and C9. Hmm.

Let's maybe not overthink; we have a template ID 95034 that matches our target. The retro step using that template likely gives a precursor. Let's use get_template to see the retro SMARTS?
